Illegal Roadblocks

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Roadblocks legal and illegal: what everybody should know

Unique Selling Point:
In the aftermath of the alleged murder of a young man at the hands of the JMPD at an illegal roadblock we examine issues surrounding roadblocks and the powers of the Police to stop and detain citizens. It is something we all have a vested interest in.

Summary:
Lobo das Neves contacted us about a case he is investigating on behalf of a family. Raymond Tzouganatos (30) was shot and killed at 20:00 on Wednesday 28 June by the Metro Police in Johannesburg. Thye initially reported that he was killed in a hijacking. Then the story changed to being killed in a shootout with the Police. Later on the story changed again when it was alleged that he was killed while tried to run over a Metro policeman. The JMPD officer involved have refused to provide statements as they are required by law, although Wayne Minnaar of the JMPD falsely said they did. It is all very fishy and it seems that the roadblock was an illegal one.
Last week a young woman was stopped at men in Police uniforms at a roadblock and raped. She stopped when commanded – something most of us would do, and paid the price.
All of the above speaks to the issue of police roadblocks and what is legal and illegal, and the rights of ordinary citizens in such cases. The big question is: Can a JMPD member or SAPS member stop anyone willy nilly? Is there something like “probable cause” in South African law? There are also cases where stops and roadblocks are illegal, for example in cases where there is no commanding officer present it is an illegal roadblock. SAPS and JMPD also claims that they are allowed to make “roadside stops”, but is that legal without “probable cause”? Lobo claims that the police actually have limited rights under the criminal procedures act, and that they cannot continue to do things as they are done currently. He also alleges that many illegal roadblocks are set up as a way to extort money from an unknowing public.

The big question is: Can a JMPD member or SAPS member stop anyone willy nilly? Is there something like “probable cause” in South African law? There are also cases where stops and roadblocks are illegal, for example in cases where there is no commanding officer present it is an illegal roadblock. SAPS and JMPD also claims that they are allowed to make “roadside stops”, but is that legal without “probable cause”? Lobo claims that the police actually have limited rights under the criminal procedures act, and that they cannot continue to do things as they are done currently. He also alleges that many illegal roadblocks are set up as a way to extort money from an unknowing public. He also have advice for people about what to look out for at roadblocks and how to spot fake ones.
In addition to exploring the Tzouganatos case and interviewing his parents, we will also confront the JMPD on the case and raise the issue of illegal roadblocks. We will also get legal advice from lawyer Rudi Krause about the articles in the criminal procedures act and the rights of the public vis a vis SAPS and JMPD officers stopping people without a reason.

Press Release:


Illegal Roadblocks
In the aftermath of the alleged murder of a young man at the hands of the Johannesburg Metro Police, Carte Blanche examines the legality of some roadblocks,
unsupervised roadside stops and the power of the police to stop and detain motorists. As thousands of drivers claim unlawful abuse by officials soliciting bribes, are
roadblocks a crime prevention measure or just another way to extort money from fearful motorists?

Script:


Diederick Stopforth:
He was very aggressive. He took my driver’s license and walked away. I followed him.

Footage and sound-up:
So this officer takes my license disk, refuses to give it to me, he has got no badge showing his ID. Can I please have you name, Sir?

V/O:
The man who had his cell phone knocked out of his hand in March this year was Diederick Stopforth. He was stopped by an Ekurhuleni Metro police officer in Edenvale, demanding a bribe. Moments later, other cops joined their colleague.

Diederick:
The one officer went as far as tapping his firearm like this, saying “We are going to teach you a lesson today”. I could see that this was gonna go wrong quickly.
V/O:
But, Stopforth kept his cool.
2.5
Diederick:
I called 10111 because I could see that need help here.
V/O:
Within minutes he could hear a siren approaching. The metro police jumped into their vehicle.

Diederick:
And they actually drove off, raced off from the scene.

V/O:
The police gave chase, but to no avail. The metro cops were gone. Stopforth laid charges of assault and theft and according to Ekurhuleni Metro Police, two officers involved have been suspended and an investigation is underway. Since March, Stopforth’s video has had more than a million views on social media.

But this is not an isolated incident.
24
LINK 1:
The very same thing happened to a young man named Raymond Tzouganatos on the 28th of June, but the outcome was very, very different.
9
V/O:
Tzouganatos, who was 30 years old at the time did not survive an altercation with the JMPD that night. He too was pulled over at a road side stop, but then 13 shots were fired. Tzouganatos died in this bakkie. His distraught family does not know what happened – just that he was killed during an informal roadblock. Elsa, Tzouganatos’ mother, is demanding answers.



Elsa Tzouganatos:
I want the truth and I want whoever did it, to pay for it. No other family must go through this, this is hell.

V/O:
Tzouganatos was killed during a road side stop where motorists are pulled over randomly by traffic police without warning or for a specific reason.

Such a stop is vastly different from an official roadblock. An official roadblock is a fairly large operation that is regulated by law, says Lobo das Neves, a law enforcement expert and former senior South African Police officer.
Lobo:
The law enforcement agency about to hold a roadblock has to make a motivated application to obtain an authorization to hold that roadblock.
V/O:
In addition, the way the roadblock is set-up and managed is also strictly regulated says Leon Louw of the Freemarket Foundation.
10
Leon Louw:
The Policing Act says there have to be proper markings on the road indicating that there is a roadblock. They can’t just wave people over. Thye have to set up a proper formal area and that has to be taped off and that has to be demarcated. There are very specific provisions in the law for how that has to be done.
V/O:
Furthermore, senior police officers must be present and officers must identify themselves and give a reason for the roadblock says criminal defence lawyer Rudi Krause.
10
Derek:
So, every roadblock has an assigned purpose to it?

Rudi:
Absolutely, and the Act also determines that of a person is stopped in such a roadblock that a person can require that the authorization of that roadblock be presented to that person.

Derek:
So, you can ask to see that certificate?

Rudi:
Absolutely, the Act states that in no uncertain terms.
V/O:
But apart from officers having to identify themselves, none of these provisions are applicable to roadside stops.
6
Leon:
A single officer or two or three, can stop a single vehicle in theory completely arbitrary, no reasons whatsoever, no grounds for suspicion, just anybody.
V/O:
Leon says these stops are highly problematic because they are random and unsupervised.
5
Leon:
Imagine what corruption and abuse this invite.
V/O:
And he is right, there are countless examples of corruption and abuse of power at these roadside stops. Motorists like Stopforth documented some on social media:

• Here a motorist is brazenly asked for a bribe…..
• In this clip another cop takes a hundred rand note from a biker.
• Here JMPD officers are filmed shoving a motorist around and unlawfully taking his vehicle. Chief Superintendent Wayne Minnaar of the JMPD has commented to News24 that what is seen here, is unacceptable behaviour.

And roadside stops are exploited by criminals who know that motorists are obliged to stop when ordered to do so by traffic officers or metro police. It creates dangerous situations, especially at night.
On the 11th of July, a woman was raped by men in uniform at 14th Avenue in Roodepoort when she followed instructions to stop.

Das Neves is adamant that these unsupervised stops have become a menace to the public.
8








5
Lobo:
Instead of being a crime prevention tool, it is a crime opportunity tool. It creates crime.
V/O:
But apart from offering an opportunity for corruption and abuse, it appears that the legislation governing these stops and the powers awarded to municipal and metro police officers could also be problematic.

Both metro police and the SAPS fall under the Criminal Procedure Act and the Police Service Act. These acts stipulate that a police officer cannot stop any person or motorist for no reason without a warrant.
24
Rudi:
A police officer and a metro police officer acting under the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act, must have reasonable grounds before a person is stopped.
V/O:
And those reasonable grounds are clearly defined in law.
Lobo:
They have to have reasonable grounds to believe that you have committed an offence to just stop you without a warrant.

Derek:
But it happens all the time.

Lobo:
And that has to stop.
V/O:
However, Chief Superintendent Wayne Minnaar of the JMPD insists that officers have the authority to conduct random stops. 7
Wayne Minnaar:
It is a standard procedure for officers in full uniform, driving fully marked cars to do a stop and search routine check. Without any offence seemingly committed by a motorist. A car can be driving perfectly well by a perfectly sober driver, the motorist can be stopped for a routine check.
V/O:
This seems to directly contradict the Police and Criminal Procedure Acts. They clearly state that a person can only be stopped when there are reasonable grounds.

This contradiction is due to Metro Police officers also operating under another Act – the National Road Traffic Act.
Article 3(i) gives traffic officers authority to stop any vehicle at any time, for no reason. These powers present a serious problem for Louw.
23
Leon:
Arbitrary powers like that could not possibly be in my view constitutional and I am awaiting as it happens a senior counsel opinion on that very matter. And the senior counsel has told me that he is provisionally satisfied that those provisions would never pass constitutional muster.
V/O:
This is because the authority granted to officers under the Road Traffic Act could infringe on an individual’s constitutional rights to freedom of movement, privacy, property and security.

Tzouganatos’s grieving parents have also decided to challenge the legality of these random stops and the powers of metro police in such instances. They have also set up a Facebook page
20
Leon:
Ever since this incident I’s heard a lot of other stories from other people and families about certain incidents that have happened with them. And here you’ve ended up being more scared more worried about the police and metro police than what you are of criminals. You know, justice has to be served. Something good has to come out of something bad. And if that means that Raymond’s incident will bring out something good, so be it. But things need to change.
V/O:
A murder docket have been opened in the Tzouganatos case.
3
Derek:
Have the officers involved in Raymond’s shooting been suspended or has other measures been taken?

Wayne:
No. Seeing that the incident is being investigated internally by the SAPS and by IPID, the officers are on duty and performing their policing function.
V/O:
It appears that current Legislation could be contradictory and this needs to be resolved. But would halting roadside stops not encourage lawless behaviour?
8
Lobo:
Not at all. It will actually have the opposite effect. There is no limitation in law as to how many roadblocks may be held. The police may apply for ten roadblocks a day. There is no limitation. When roadblocks are properly monitored the chances for corruption and crime will decline dramatically which will change the drivers’ mind on how to use the road and take away the idea and perception that you can get away with your bad driving by putting a fifty rand note out the window.

These powers present a serious problem for Louw. 23 Leon: Arbitrary powers like that could not possibly be in my view constitutional and I am awaiting as it happens a senior counsel opinion on that very matter. And the senior counsel has told me that he is provisionally satisfied that those provisions would never pass constitutional muster. V/O: This is because the authority granted to officers under the Road Traffic Act could infringe on an individual’s constitutional rights to freedom of movement, privacy, property and security. Tzouganatos’s grieving parents have also decided to challenge the legality of these random stops and the powers of metro police in such instances. They have also set up a Facebook page 20 Leon: Ever since this incident I’s heard a lot of other stories from other people and families about certain incidents that have happened with them. And here you’ve ended up being more scared more worried about the police and metro police than what you are of criminals. You know, justice has to be served. Something good has to come out of something bad. And if that means that Raymond’s incident will bring out something good, so be it. But things need to change. V/O: A murder docket have been opened in the Tzouganatos case. 3 Derek: Have the officers involved in Raymond’s shooting been suspended or has other measures been taken? Wayne: No. Seeing that the incident is being investigated internally by the SAPS and by IPID, the officers are on duty and performing their policing function. V/O: It appears that current Legislation could be contradictory and this needs to be resolved. But would halting roadside stops not encourage lawless behaviour? 8 Lobo: Not at all. It will actually have the opposite effect. There is no limitation in law as to how many roadblocks may be held. The police may apply for ten roadblocks a day. There is no limitation. When roadblocks are properly monitored the chances for corruption and crime will decline dramatically which will change the drivers’ mind on how to use the road and take away the idea and perception that you can get away with your bad driving by putting a fifty rand note out the window.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Roadblocks legal and illegal: what everybody should know
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In the aftermath of the alleged murder of a young man at the hands of the JMPD at an illegal roadblock we examine issues surrounding roadblocks and the powers of the Police to stop and detain citizens. It is something we all have a vested interest in.
metadata.Summary: Lobo das Neves contacted us about a case he is investigating on behalf of a family. Raymond Tzouganatos (30) was shot and killed at 20:00 on Wednesday 28 June by the Metro Police in Johannesburg. Thye initially reported that he was killed in a hijacking. Then the story changed to being killed in a shootout with the Police. Later on the story changed again when it was alleged that he was killed while tried to run over a Metro policeman. The JMPD officer involved have refused to provide statements as they are required by law, although Wayne Minnaar of the JMPD falsely said they did. It is all very fishy and it seems that the roadblock was an illegal one. Last week a young woman was stopped at men in Police uniforms at a roadblock and raped. She stopped when commanded – something most of us would do, and paid the price. All of the above speaks to the issue of police roadblocks and what is legal and illegal, and the rights of ordinary citizens in such cases. The big question is: Can a JMPD member or SAPS member stop anyone willy nilly? Is there something like “probable cause” in South African law? There are also cases where stops and roadblocks are illegal, for example in cases where there is no commanding officer present it is an illegal roadblock. SAPS and JMPD also claims that they are allowed to make “roadside stops”, but is that legal without “probable cause”? Lobo claims that the police actually have limited rights under the criminal procedures act, and that they cannot continue to do things as they are done currently. He also alleges that many illegal roadblocks are set up as a way to extort money from an unknowing public.
